c.v: For twenty years a fall on someone else’s property in Michigan was close to unwinnable, because a hazard that was “open and obvious” ended the case before it began. That rule is gone. Since the Michigan Supreme Court’s July 2023 decision in
Kandil-Elsayed v F & E Oil

, a Clinton Township fall case turns on who had the duty to keep the place safe, what they knew about the hazard and when, what they did about it, and how much of the fall was your fault. In Clinton Township those questions have local answers: Partridge Creek’s outdoor walkways and parking lots, and the big-box stores and restaurants along Hall Road; the strip centers and dealerships on Gratiot; apartment, condominium, and senior communities along Gratiot, Fifteen Mile, Garfield, and Harper, where an association or a management company controls the walks; the industrial buildings and warehouses on Groesbeck; schools, the community college, and township buildings, each with a 120-day notice rule; and sidewalks, which the township must maintain even though it owns none of the roads beside them.

sections.heading: Where Clinton Township falls happen, and who is responsible

c.v: Partridge Creek and the Hall Road stores.

Partridge Creek is an outdoor center, so its walkways, crosswalks, and parking lots are exposed to snow, ice, and meltwater in a way an enclosed mall’s corridors are not. The big-box stores, grocery stores, and restaurants along Hall Road add spills, freshly mopped floors without signs, merchandise in the aisle, ice at entrances, and potholes and broken curbs in the lots. A shopper is an invitee: a property owner or possessor must exercise reasonable care under the circumstances, which may include inspecting for hazards, correcting dangerous conditions, or providing appropriate warnings. The case is decided on
notice

, actual (an employee saw or caused it) or constructive (it existed long enough that a reasonable inspection would have found it). At a shopping center, the center’s owner and management company usually control the common walks, decks, and lots, the tenant store controls its own floor, and a snow-removal or maintenance contractor may share the duty; the leases and service contracts decide who, so we request them with the footage.
Gratiot’s strip centers and dealerships.

Small retail plazas, restaurants, and dealership showrooms and service drives along Gratiot: icy walks between parking and doors, broken pavement in shared lots, oil and fluids on service-area floors, and poorly lit lots at night. The lease decides whether the business or the plaza owner maintained the lot and the walk.
Apartments, condominiums, and senior communities.

Clinton Township has large apartment complexes along Gratiot, Fifteen Mile, Garfield, and Harper, condominium communities throughout, and many senior apartment, independent living, and assisted living communities. In a condominium, the association, not the unit owner, usually controls the common walks, stairs, and lots, and its snow-removal contract and maintenance records are the evidence. Landlords must keep the premises and common areas fit for their intended use and in reasonable repair (MCL 554.139): broken stairs, loose handrails, dark stairwells and parking lots, and failed lighting are the usual claims. A lot with an inch or two of snow is still “fit” for parking under
Allison v AEW Capital
(2008), so tenant snow cases depend on whether the accumulation actually prevented use; the general negligence claim after
Kandil-Elsayed

is a separate route. A lease clause waiving the landlord’s liability for its own negligence is void. Older residents who fall often suffer hip and wrist fractures and head injuries that change their lives, and a fall in an assisted living community may be a care claim as well as a premises claim. Groesbeck’s warehouses and industrial buildings.

A truck driver, delivery driver, staffing-agency worker, or contractor who falls at a Groesbeck warehouse, yard, or plant is not that facility’s employee. Their own employer’s workers’ compensation pays their benefits, and the facility owner or the general contractor that controlled the dock, the yard, or the icy lot can be sued as a third party. The comp insurer is repaid from that recovery (MCL 418.827). The facility’s own employee generally cannot sue the employer (MCL 418.131), but may have a claim against a contractor whose work created the hazard; a worker placed by a staffing agency may be treated as the facility’s employee too. See our
workers’ compensation page
Sidewalks: the township, even though it does not own the roads.

Clinton Township has no jurisdiction over its roads, which belong to the Macomb County Department of Roads and MDOT. Sidewalks are different. Under the immunity act a township is a “municipal corporation,” and the municipal corporation in which a sidewalk runs beside a county or state road must keep that sidewalk in reasonable repair (MCL 691.1401(d), 691.1402a(1)). The duties of the State and the county under the highway exception stop at the roadway (MCL 691.1402(1)). So a fall on a broken public sidewalk along Gratiot, Hall Road, Garfield, or Romeo Plank is generally a claim against Clinton Township, not the county or MDOT. The township must have known, or should have known, of the defect at least 30 days before the fall; a defect under two inches is presumed to be reasonable repair unless the evidence shows otherwise, and the judge decides whether the presumption is rebutted (MCL 691.1402a(2)–(4)). Measure and photograph the defect with a ruler before it is patched, and serve written notice on the township stating the exact location, the defect, the injury, and the witnesses within 120 days (MCL 691.1404). A sidewalk inside a shopping center, apartment complex, or condominium community belongs to its owner or association, and the claim is an ordinary premises claim.
Schools, the college, township buildings, and parks.

Clinton Township is served mainly by the Chippewa Valley and Clintondale school districts, with parts in L’Anse Creuse, Fraser, and Mount Clemens. Each is a governmental agency, and so is Macomb Community College, whose Center Campus is on Hall Road: a fall caused by a dangerous or defective condition of one of their buildings proceeds under the public building exception, which requires the agency to have known of the defect and failed to fix it, with written notice within 120 days (MCL 691.1406). The same rule applies to the township’s civic center and other township buildings and to the public library. A fall on a township park path or field, outside a building, has no comparable exception and is difficult to bring.
The hospital and nursing homes.

A visitor’s fall at Henry Ford Macomb Hospital or a medical office on the hospital campus is a premises claim. A patient’s fall, or a resident’s fall in one of the township’s three Medicare-certified nursing homes, may be premises, negligence, or medical malpractice, and which one decides the deadline. sections.heading: A parking-lot fall can be a no-fault claim

c.v: If you fell while getting into or out of your own car, or while loading it, Michigan’s no-fault law may cover your medical bills and lost wages even though no crash occurred. An injury from a parked vehicle is covered when the person was “occupying, entering into, or alighting from” it, or was injured by property being lifted onto or lowered from it during loading or unloading (MCL 500.3106(1)). That claim runs on the no-fault notice rules: written notice to the auto insurer within one year (MCL 500.3145(1)). It sits alongside any premises claim against the lot’s or parking deck’s owner. A worker hurt on the job while loading, unloading, or getting into or out of a parked vehicle is generally limited to workers’ compensation for that injury, with narrow exceptions (MCL 500.3106(2)).
Under the old rule (
Lugo v Ameritech
, 2001), an owner owed no duty to protect visitors from a danger an average person would have noticed, and insurers denied fall claims on that basis. In
Kandil-Elsayed v F & E Oil

(Michigan Supreme Court, July 28, 2023), the Court held that whether a hazard was open and obvious no longer decides whether a duty existed. It is now a factor in whether the owner breached the duty of reasonable care, and in how much of the fault belongs to the person who fell; both are questions for a jury. That does not make every fall a case. A visible hazard still matters: if the jury assigns you some fault, your damages are reduced by that share, and above half you recover no pain-and-suffering damages, only reduced economic losses (MCL 600.2959).

Duty also depends on why you were there. A shopper, tenant, or business visitor is an invitee, owed inspection and repair; a social guest at a home is a licensee, owed a warning of hidden dangers the owner knows about; a trespasser is owed protection from willful and wanton misconduct. Treating every visitor the same overstates or understates the claim.

An owner must take reasonable steps, within a reasonable time after snow or ice accumulates, to make walkways, entrances, parking decks, and lots safe. What is reasonable depends on the property: a grocery store opening at 7 a.m. after an overnight storm is expected to have treated its entrance, an outdoor center like Partridge Creek its walks and crosswalks, and an apartment complex its stairs and paths before residents leave for work. A contractor with a salting contract that missed the morning run may share the fault. The law does not require an owner to keep every surface bare at every moment of a storm. Black ice from refreezing meltwater, a leaking gutter or downspout, or snow piled where it melts across the walk can be a condition the owner created, and those cases are stronger than natural accumulation.
Some Michigan communities require adjacent owners to clear snow and ice from public sidewalks by ordinance. Photograph the ice, the path, the alternatives you had, and the weather the same day.

faqs.question: I slipped on ice on a walkway at Partridge Creek. Who is responsible?

answer.v: Usually the center’s owner and its management company, which control the common walks, and possibly their snow-removal contractor. Since 2023, an obvious hazard no longer ends the case; the questions are whether the walk should have been treated by the time you arrived, whether you had a realistic alternative route, and how much of the fault is yours.

faqs.question: I fell on a broken sidewalk along Gratiot. Is that MDOT’s responsibility?

answer.v: Generally not. MDOT owns Gratiot, but its duty stops at the roadway; Clinton Township must keep the public sidewalk beside it in reasonable repair. The township must have known or should have known of the defect at least 30 days before, defects under two inches are presumed reasonable repair, and written notice must reach the township within 120 days.

faqs.question: My mother fell in her apartment complex’s stairwell. Do we have a case?

answer.v: Possibly. A landlord must keep stairs and common areas in reasonable repair and fit for their use, and a general negligence claim may apply too. Broken stairs, loose handrails, and failed lighting are the usual claims, and the complex’s maintenance requests and prior complaints are the evidence.

faqs.question: I deliver for a trucking company and fell on the ice at a Groesbeck warehouse. Can I sue the facility?

answer.v: Possibly. Your employer’s workers’ compensation pays your benefits, and the facility owner or the contractor that controlled the yard or dock where you fell can be sued as a third party. The comp insurer is repaid from that recovery.

faqs.question: I fell getting out of my car in a parking lot. Is that a car accident claim?

answer.v: It may be. No-fault can cover injuries from entering or leaving a parked vehicle, separate from any claim against the lot’s owner.
Three years to sue a private owner; 120 days for written notice to the township, a school district, or the college; and one year to notify a no-fault insurer. The footage disappears far sooner.
